props.title: High Crimes
props.initialSlug: Justice can be a deadly game.

sections.content: High Crimes stands as a taut military legal thriller that reunites Ashley Judd and Morgan Freeman after their successful pairing in Kiss the Girls (1997). The film follows civilian defense attorney Claire Kubik (Judd) who discovers her husband's secret past as a military operative accused of massacring civilians in El Salvador. The movie builds on a tradition of military justice films like A Few Good Men (1992) and Rules of Engagement (2000), but adds layers of conspiracy and personal betrayal that elevate it beyond standard courtroom drama.

sections.content: The film particularly excels in its exploration of military justice systems and their opacity to civilian oversight. Like The General's Daughter (1999), it peels back layers of military culture while maintaining suspense. Director Carl Franklin, who previously directed the noir-tinged Devil in a Blue Dress (1995), brings a similar sense of mounting paranoia and conspiracy to this military thriller, though working in a more mainstream format.

The chemistry between Judd and Freeman echoes classic legal partnerships like Presumed Innocent (1990) and Primal Fear (1996). Their dynamic drives the investigation forward as they uncover increasingly disturbing truths about military cover-ups and covert operations, themes that would later be explored in films like Rendition (2007) and Lions for Lambs (2007). sections.content: High Crimes fits into a larger pattern of post-Cold War films examining military accountability, alongside works like The Hunt for Red October (1990) and Crimson Tide (1995). These films share a common thread of questioning chain of command and military authority, while maintaining respect for service members caught in moral dilemmas. The film's exploration of classified operations and their consequences prefigured later works like Green Zone (2010) and Body of Lies (2008).
